title: Data Integrity: What You Read Is What You Wrote
subtitle: Prove that correct user data can be restored in time
summary: Pip verifies a backup checksum and discovers that restoring usable bookings takes far too long. Recovery needs compatible data, metadata, capacity, and application access. Independent protection and early invariant checks help preserve a recovery point that actually works.

concepts.title: Recovery as the objective
concepts.body: Pip’s export passes its checksum but rebuilding indexes exceeds the acceptable outage. Disaster recovery means the application can load and serve data, not merely retain an archive. Pip defines tolerated data loss and waiting time. The restore test includes capacity, dependencies, format compatibility, and post-processing through real user access.

concepts.title: Independent layers of protection
concepts.body: Pip’s accidental deletion reaches every replica. Replication propagates bad changes as well as good ones. Soft deletion and tiered backups offer different undo windows and isolated older recovery points. Pip designs independence against common failures while keeping retention and deletion delays consistent with privacy commitments.

concepts.title: Early validation of application invariants
concepts.body: Pip finds metadata pointing to missing audio before another backup cycle copies the defect. Storage consistency does not guarantee application relationships. Independent validators check product-defined invariants with ownership, monitoring, logs, and rate limits. Pip detects slow corruption early without overloading the service that the checks protect.

concepts.title: Restore engineering at scale
concepts.body: Pip parallelizes restore across balanced shards and verifies that recovered objects are reachable in the application. Incremental processing speeds large datasets, but long dependent backup chains add recovery complexity and failure exposure. Data and metadata must come from compatible points. Pip rehearses end to end to reveal missing media, capacity shortages, broken tools, and schema drift.

misconceptions.claim: A successful backup job proves that recovery works.
misconceptions.correction: Only a tested restore through to usable application data verifies the complete recovery path.

scenario.title: Prove what users received
scenario.context: A replicated profile store returns data after a regional failover. A checksum mismatch appears on one replica, but serving traffic is still possible from two healthy copies.

options.label: Quarantine the mismatched replica and validate before repair
options.benefit: Users read from verified copies and the corruption boundary stays known.
options.cost: The healthy copies carry more load during validation.
options.consequence: The team routes around the replica, verifies checksums, and rebuilds it.

options.label: Accept the replica and repair asynchronously
options.benefit: Availability remains high and repair starts immediately.
options.cost: Bad data can spread or be read before repair completes.
options.consequence: A later read exposes corrupted profile data to customers.

scenario.debrief: Isolating a suspect copy prevents unverified data from reaching users, but replica repair covers only some failure modes. Also test recovery from application corruption that reaches every replica, including restoring coherent data and metadata.

quiz.question: Which failure can ordinary synchronous replication spread?
options: Loss of the only historical snapshot after all live replicas stay correct
A site outage that leaves healthy remote replicas reachable
quiz.explanation: Replication deliberately propagates mutations, including harmful ones.

quiz.question: Why is early detection especially valuable for creeping corruption?
options: It makes historical backups unnecessary for application errors
It lets validators scan without competing for serving resources
It limits propagation and preserves more usable recovery points
quiz.explanation: Delay makes both the affected state and the reconstruction problem grow.

quiz.question: What is the strongest evidence that a backup strategy meets its purpose?
options: A full backup completing within the nightly maintenance window
An end-to-end restore delivering correct accessible data within the target time
Every replica reporting the same current database size
quiz.explanation: The required outcome is usable restored data, not a successfully written file.
